planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in gritty, sharply drained soil; unlike most snowdrops this species flowers in autumn before its leaves emerge, so give it a dry summer rest.

directions: Plant dormant bulbs in late summer in sharply drained, humus-rich soil at the base of deciduous shrubs or in a rock garden pocket that bakes dry over summer. Native to limestone cliffs and rocky slopes of southern Turkey and the Greek island of Karpathos, this unusual snowdrop breaks dormancy in autumn and sends up slender white flowers weeks or months before its leaves appear, a trait almost no other Galanthus shares. Give it winter and spring moisture but a dry, warm summer rest to mimic its native Mediterranean cycle, and site it where fallen leaves or taller perennials will not hide the early blooms. It resents being disturbed once settled, so choose a permanent spot rather than planning to divide it often.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this species from southern Turkey flowers in late autumn to winter, often with its narrow leaves already showing.

directions: Plant dormant bulbs in late summer to early fall in gritty, well-drained soil in a sheltered, partly shaded spot such as beneath deciduous shrubs. Named for the Cilicia region of southern Turkey where it grows among limestone scrub, this species is closely related to the better-known autumn snowdrop Galanthus peshmenii but typically shows its narrow leaves alongside the flowers rather than well before them. It prefers a warm, dry summer dormancy followed by cool, moist conditions through winter and early spring. Because it resents root disturbance, plant it where it can be left undivided for years and mulch lightly to protect the crowns through hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this species, native to the Troad region of northwestern Turkey, flowers in winter into early spring.

directions: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. This species, formally described in 2001, takes its name from the ancient Troad region of northwestern Turkey, where it grows in woodland and scrub at relatively low elevation. It behaves much like other woodland snowdrops, pushing up slender white flowers in late winter and bulking up gradually by offsets once established in a cool, humus-rich site. Division is rarely needed in the first several years; when clumps do become congested, lift and replant them in the green right after flowering.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this species from the forests of northeastern Turkey belongs to the alpinus clade and flowers in late winter to early spring.

directions: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full to partial shade beneath deciduous woodland canopy. Native to montane forest in northeastern Turkey, this snowdrop belongs to the same alpinus group as Galanthus alpinus and shares its preference for cool summers and consistent woodland humidity rather than the drier, baking conditions some other Turkish snowdrops tolerate. It is still uncommon in cultivation outside specialist bulb collections, so source bulbs from a reputable nursery rather than wild-collected stock. Once established it increases slowly by offsets; leave clumps undisturbed for several years before dividing in the green after flowering.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; native to the Caucasus and northern Iran, it belongs to the same alpinus group as the common snowdrop's relatives and flowers in late winter to early spring.

directions: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. This species grows wild across the Caucasus region and into northern Iran, occupying woodland and scrub habitats somewhat differently than the common snowdrop, Galanthus nivalis, to which it is closely related. It sends up its slender white flowers in late winter to early spring and gradually forms small colonies by bulb offsets once settled into a cool, humus-rich site. Mulch with leaf litter in fall to replicate its natural woodland floor and avoid letting the planting site dry out completely during the growing season.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; native to beech and hornbeam forest in Georgia's Lagodekhi region, it belongs to the same woronowii group as the green-leaved Galanthus woronowii and flowers in early spring.

directions: Plant dormant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full to partial shade beneath deciduous forest canopy. Named for the Lagodekhi area of the Caucasus in eastern Georgia, where it grows on the forest floor beneath beech and hornbeam, this snowdrop belongs to the same group as the glossy green-leaved Galanthus woronowii. Its bright green, relatively broad leaves and clean white flowers appear in early spring, and it performs best where summers stay cool and humid rather than hot and dry. Let colonies spread undisturbed for several seasons, dividing clumps in the green only once they become noticeably congested.
